title: IAEA Says It Cannot Verify Isfahan Enrichment Plant or Rule Out Nuclear Material Diversion
dek: A confidential IAEA report circulated Friday says the agency does not know the location or status of an underground Isfahan enrichment plant Iran declared in 2025, and cannot rule out diversion.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: The Vienna International Centre, which houses the headquarters of the International Atomic Energy Agency
image.credit: IAEA Imagebank (Rodolfo Quevenco/IAEA), via Wikimedia Commons

keyPoints: A confidential IAEA report circulated Friday says the agency is “increasingly concerned” about an underground enrichment plant near Isfahan.
The agency says it does not know the plant’s exact location, safeguards status or whether it contains nuclear material.
Grossi wrote that the agency “is not able to conclude that there has been no diversion” of declared nuclear material.
Iran told the agency inspections cannot resume amid U.S. threats; the report did not establish that enrichment is taking place at the site.
body:
The United Nations nuclear watchdog said Friday that it is “increasingly concerned” about an underground uranium enrichment plant near Isfahan that Iran has declared but has not allowed inspectors to visit. The concern is set out in a confidential report circulated among member states. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said the lack of information about Iran’s nuclear sites and material is “a matter of proliferation concern” that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency,” [Al Jazeera reported](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/13/un-watchdog-calls-on-iran-to-reopen-nuclear-facilities-to-inspection), citing AP.

## What the agency does not know

According to the 13-page document circulated in Vienna on Friday, the agency “does not know IFEP’s exact location, status for safeguards purposes or whether it contains nuclear material.” IFEP is the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant, which Iran declared in 2025 ([The National](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2026/11/13/iaea-expresses-concern-over-iranian-underground-uranium-enrichment-plant/)).

The report did not establish that uranium enrichment is taking place at the site, Al Jazeera reported, citing AFP, AP and Reuters. The agency also said it could not determine whether any nuclear material had been diverted from peaceful activities.

Director General Rafael Grossi wrote in the report that “it is more than a year since the agency lost continuity of knowledge in relation to the previously declared inventories of highly enriched uranium.” He added that the agency “is not able to conclude that there has been no diversion of declared nuclear material from peaceful nuclear activities,” according to the report as quoted by The National.

## Access requests and Iran’s position

The IAEA requested access to the site in February, and Iran declined, [Vatican News reported](https://www.vaticannews.va/en/world/news/2026-11/un-nuclear-agency-iran-uranium-concern.html). Iran has allowed only very limited IAEA inspections since the United States and Israel attacked its nuclear facilities in June 2025, Al Jazeera reported.

Iran told the agency this month that discussion of resuming inspections cannot proceed amid what it described as “persistent, explicit, and public threats” by the U.S. president to commit further acts of armed aggression. According to the report, Tehran said the issue would not be resolved “until the root causes of the present situation are addressed.”

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday that Iran remained committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. He blamed U.S. and Israeli attacks for limiting cooperation with the IAEA, Al Jazeera reported.

## Rewards and rhetoric

Iran’s national security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said Iran would not allow “a single particle” of enriched nuclear material to leave the country. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi asked the agency and the United Nations to condemn a U.S. offer of a $20 million reward for information on Tehran’s nuclear programme, The National reported.

The State Department said the reward is for details on Iran’s nuclear facilities, equipment and associated personnel, including scientists and their whereabouts.

## Background

U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran’s nuclear programme was “obliterated” by the joint U.S. and Israeli strikes in June 2025, The National reported. The agency estimates Iran had produced more than 400 kilograms of near weapons-grade enriched uranium before those attacks. It is not clear what happened to that material.

Inspectors were withdrawn for safety reasons after the strikes, and Iran later passed a law suspending cooperation with the agency, Al Jazeera reported. The IAEA said it is “fully prepared to resume its safeguards activities in Iran at short notice.” Grossi has urged Tehran to consider limited technical measures that could make inspection visits possible, AFP reported.

Meridian has relied on press accounts of the report. The full document was not available to us, so the figures and quotations above are as reported by the outlets cited.
